prompt: Statements about linked lists — which one is correct?
options: Inserting two elements consecutively at the end of a singly linked list requires at most two traversals of the list.
Every element of a singly linked list contains at least two pointers.
Singly linked lists allow direct access to an arbitrary element by index.
In a singly linked list one can iterate backwards through the list.
explanation: Without a tail pointer each append walks from the head to the end — one traversal per insert, hence at most two for two inserts. A singly linked node holds exactly one pointer (next), there is no index access, and without prev pointers backward iteration is impossible.

prompt: Linked lists and abstract data types — which two statements are correct?
options: An advantage of linked lists is that insert and delete work by adjusting pointers, without shifting the remaining elements.
In a doubly linked list each element holds a pointer only to the next element.
An ADT describes the possible values, operations and behaviour of a data type, but not its concrete implementation.
The ADT description specifies the time complexity of the operations on linked lists.
explanation: No shifting is exactly the structural advantage over arrays ✓, and an ADT is an implementation-agnostic contract ✓. A doubly linked node holds *both* next and prev ✗, and complexity follows from the chosen implementation, not from the ADT ✗.

prompt: Given only a pointer to the node to be removed, deletion is Θ(1) in a doubly linked list but Θ(n) in a singly linked list. Which statement gives the reason?
options: Doubly linked lists are always shorter than singly linked ones.
The prev pointer makes it unnecessary to walk from the head to find the predecessor.
Singly linked lists do not support deletion at all.
In a singly linked list the successor pointer must be recomputed for every remaining node.
explanation: With prev available you can directly relink predecessor and successor in constant time. Without it, the predecessor — whose next pointer must be redirected — can only be found by scanning from the head, which costs Θ(n).

prompt: Array versus linked list — which two statements are correct?
options: Random access A[i] is Θ(1) in an array and Θ(n) in a linked list.
Inserting at a known position is Θ(n) in an array (shifting) and Θ(1) in a linked list.
A linked list uses less memory per element than an array, because it needs no contiguous block.
Searching for a value is Θ(log n) in an unsorted linked list.
explanation: These are the two defining trade-offs ✓✓. A linked list uses *more* memory per element — each node carries pointer overhead on top of the value ✗ — and unsorted search is Θ(n), since binary search needs random access ✗.

prompt: Sentinels (Wächter) in linked lists — which two statements are correct?
options: A sentinel is a permanent dummy node that removes the need to special-case the empty list and the list boundaries.
With a sentinel, every real node always has a valid prev/next to link against.
A sentinel reduces the asymptotic cost of search from Θ(n) to Θ(log n).
A sentinel stores the length of the list so that size queries become Θ(1).
explanation: The sentinel's purpose is purely to eliminate boundary special cases ✓✓ — it trades slightly more complex initialization for simpler insert/delete code. It changes no asymptotics ✗ and is not a length counter ✗.

prompt: `RemoveDuplicates` on a singly linked list uses a reference pointer a and a scanning pointer b, in O(1) extra space. Which two statements are correct?
options: When b.next.key == a.key, the duplicate is spliced out via b.next = b.next.next.
The runtime is O(n²), because the inner scan runs (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 times in the worst case.
The algorithm needs an auxiliary hash set to remember which values have been seen.
The runtime is O(n), because each node is visited exactly once.
explanation: Splicing past the duplicate is the O(1) removal step ✓, and fixing each reference against everything ahead of it gives the arithmetic series ⟹ Θ(n²) ✓. Avoiding a hash set is precisely what forces the quadratic scan ✗✗.

prompt: The loop invariant of `RemoveDuplicates` (outer loop over a) — which two statements are correct?
options: Before the i-th outer iteration, the sublist from the head up to and including a contains no duplicates.
At termination (a = nil) every node has served as reference point, so the list contains only unique values.
The invariant guarantees that the list is sorted after each outer iteration.
Initialization fails, because a one-element sublist cannot be shown to be duplicate-free.
explanation: The duplicate-free-prefix invariant ✓ combined with the exit condition yields the postcondition ✓. The algorithm never reorders anything, so sortedness is not claimed ✗, and a single-element sublist is trivially duplicate-free, so initialization holds ✗.
